questions.q: What basic question does version control exist to help answer, per this lesson?
options: How fast can a program run
Which programming language is being used
How many developers are on a team
What changed in the code, when, and why -- a question overwriting a file in place destroys the ability to answer
questions.explain: The lesson frames version control as solving exactly this problem: overwriting code in place destroys history, while version control records every change as an inspectable, comparable, revertible snapshot.

questions.q: What is a 'commit,' as this lesson defines it?
options: The entire tracked history of a codebase from its first snapshot onward
A deliberate, labeled checkpoint recording exactly what the code looked like at that moment, along with a message describing what changed and why
A separate, parallel line of development that diverges from the main history
A tool used exclusively for Salesforce development
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes a repository (the full history) from a commit (one specific labeled snapshot with an accompanying message) from a branch (a parallel line of commits) -- a commit is specifically the single checkpoint.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'Fixed bug' is a weak commit message compared to 'Fixed off-by-one error in discount loop that skipped the last order item'?
options: Because 'Fixed bug' answers nothing a quick look at the code diff wouldn't already show, while the specific message names the actual problem independent of re-deriving it from the code
Because 'Fixed bug' is grammatically incorrect
Because commit messages must always be at least ten words long
Because only the second message is allowed by Git
questions.explain: The lesson's point is that a vague message adds no information beyond the diff itself, while a specific message communicates the actual problem to a future reader who has no other context -- a communication skill, not an afterthought.

questions.q: What real problem does branching solve, per this lesson?
options: It prevents a codebase from ever needing a commit message
It deletes old commits to save storage space
It lets risky or incomplete work happen in isolation, off to the side, so the main history everyone depends on stays stable until the new work is actually ready to rejoin it
It converts a repository into a single file
questions.explain: The lesson explains that working on an incomplete change directly in the shared main history means anyone looking at it mid-change sees broken work -- a branch isolates that risk until the work is ready to merge back.

questions.q: Why does this lesson teach version control concepts generically, independent of a specific tool like Git?
options: Because Git is being phased out of the software industry

Because the underlying ideas -- not a specific command syntax -- are what transfer, and a later course in this path builds directly on these same concepts using Git for Salesforce's own developer tooling
Because Salesforce does not use version control at all
Because tool-specific commands are more important to learn first than the concepts
questions.explain: The lesson explains that it deliberately teaches the concepts (repository, commit, history, branch) rather than tool-specific syntax, because those concepts transfer and are built on directly by a later course covering Salesforce DX and Git-based tooling.
